run.question: We noticed our metrics dashboard shows missing data. Can you analyze the app-189-metrics-timeseries index to find any gaps in the data collection? When did data stop being collected and when did it resume? Also, what was the last request ID before the gap started?

report.summary: The index app-189-metrics-timeseries contains exactly 42 documents, all with metric_name=cpu_usage, written hourly at :47:00 by hosts server-1 through server-5, spanning 2026-11-21T18:47:00Z to 2026-11-23T17:47:00Z; it is the only index in the Elasticsearch target. One collection gap sits inside that series: the last document before the gap is at 2026-11-23T07:47:00Z and the next after it at 2026-11-23T14:47:00Z, and the hourly histogram has zero documents in the six buckets 2026-11-23T08:00Z, 09:00Z, 10:00Z, 11:00Z, 12:00Z and 13:00Z, so the six expected :47 samples for 08:47 through 13:47 UTC are absent. Collection therefore stopped after the 07:47:00Z sample and resumed at 14:47:00Z. The last request_id before the gap is REQ-37-8A4F2 (host server-3, value 77.0, @timestamp 2026-11-23T07:47:00Z), which is the only request_id in the index that does not follow the REQ-NNNN-NNNN pattern of the other 41 documents. Every pod in the cluster, including otel-collector-69c9f9649-vdpcn, reports 0 restarts and startTime between 2026-11-23T14:36:08Z and 2026-11-23T14:38:05Z, so the environment observed at query time was created about nine minutes before the 14:47 sample. The same collector pod logs a recurring 'failed to upload metrics ... http2: frame too large' error every ~10s at 17:47-17:48, but that is not tied to the gap because hourly index samples exist at 14:47, 15:47, 16:47 and 17:47 while those errors occur. What stopped the writer between 07:47 and 14:47 is not evidenced: the pre-gap collector instance no longer exists, its previous-container logs are unavailable, and no Kubernetes events were returned. No root-cause object can be named on this evidence.

claims.text: app-189-metrics-timeseries holds 42 documents in the authorized window; every document has metric_name=cpu_usage; hosts are server-1 through server-5; the first @timestamp is 2026-11-21T18:47:00.000Z and the last is 2026-11-23T17:47:00.000Z. The index is the only index in the Elasticsearch target (docs.count 42).

The series is an hourly series sampled at :47:00. The 1h date_histogram over the whole authorized window returns doc_count 1 for every hour from 2026-11-21T18:00Z through 2026-11-23T07:00Z and from 2026-11-23T14:00Z through 2026-11-23T17:00Z, and doc_count 0 for the buckets 2026-11-23T08:00Z, 2026-11-23T09:00Z, 2026-11-23T10:00Z, 2026-11-23T11:00Z, 2026-11-23T12:00Z and 2026-11-23T13:00Z.

Data collection stopped after the sample at @timestamp 2026-11-23T07:47:00Z and resumed with the sample at @timestamp 2026-11-23T14:47:00Z, leaving the six expected hourly samples 08:47, 09:47, 10:47, 11:47, 12:47 and 13:47 UTC on 2026-11-23 absent.

The last request_id before the gap is REQ-37-8A4F2, in the document at 2026-11-23T07:47:00Z with host server-3 and value 77.0; it is the only request_id in the index whose format differs from the REQ-NNNN-NNNN pattern of the other 41 documents, for example REQ-1231-7934 at 06:47:00Z and REQ-2027-5414 at 14:47:00Z.

Per-host document counts in the index are server-1 9, server-2 9, server-3 9, server-5 8 and server-4 7; the hourly sample alternates through server-1 through server-5, showing server-3 at 07:47:00Z and server-5 at 14:47:00Z across the gap.

All 32 pods in the cluster report 0 restarts with startTime between 2026-11-23T14:36:08Z and 2026-11-23T14:38:05Z, including otel-collector-69c9f9649-vdpcn (startTime 2026-11-23T14:38:02Z, phase Running), prometheus-9bc78b5f7-k84v7 (14:38:03Z) and kube-state-metrics-7cbf5b996-vbw5s (14:38:03Z); this is the state at query time, about nine minutes before the first post-gap sample at 14:47:00Z.

The current otel-collector-69c9f9649-vdpcn container emits 'failed to upload metrics: reader collect and export timeout: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = connection error: desc = "error reading server preface: http2: failed reading the frame payload: http2: frame too large, note that the frame header looked like an HTTP/1.1 header"' repeatedly at roughly 10 second intervals (17:47:18.419779908Z, 17:47:28.420440487Z, 17:47:38.421240716Z, 17:47:48.420721493Z, 17:47:58.419936668Z, 17:48:08.420669467Z) while the same pod also logs successful Metrics, Traces and Logs exports.

The collector's recurring 'failed to upload metrics' errors do not explain the index gap: documents were still written to app-189-metrics-timeseries at 14:47:00Z, 15:47:00Z, 16:47:00Z and 17:47:00Z while those errors were active, so an upload failure of this kind is not a demonstrated cause of the six missing 08:47-13:47 samples.

The most likely operational explanation is that the environment was torn down after the 07:47:00Z sample and recreated just before collection resumed: every pod present now started at 14:36-14:38 UTC with zero restarts, and the first post-gap index sample is 14:47:00Z. This is timing correlation only; no evidence shows when the previous cluster or its writer stopped.

A second unresolved candidate is a write or export outage in the metrics pipeline feeding this index, for example the collector's metrics exporter endpoint behind the 'failed to upload metrics' error. The sampled collector evidence shows such failures only for the post-14:38 pod and only at 17:47-17:48, so it is not confirmed that the same failure existed during 08:47-13:47.

The off-pattern request_id REQ-37-8A4F2 on the last pre-gap record may be a malformed or corrupted sample rather than a normally generated ID, since all 41 other documents use the REQ-NNNN-NNNN format. Nothing in the evidence shows this record caused the gap; it is a data-quality observation adjacent in time to the gap.

A retention or rollover boundary is not the explanation of the observed gap: the index begins at 2026-11-21T18:47:00Z and its 42 documents equal the full docs.count of the index, so the only mid-series interruption observed is the 2026-11-23T08:47-13:47 UTC block rather than a start-of-series truncation.

gaps: The Kubernetes events query across all namespaces returned status no_data with 0 items processed, so no event evidence explains what happened to the collector or cluster at 2026-11-23T07:47-14:47Z; absent events are unknown, not proof that nothing happened.

The collector instance that wrote the pre-gap samples no longer exists: fetch_pod_logs for otel-collector-69c9f9649-vdpcn reported 'previous terminated container ... not found', and the evidence view for that log read is marked incomplete (newest 80 of 6182 matching lines shown), so the reason collection stopped cannot be read from logs.

Whether the six empty hourly buckets reflect a writer or collection outage versus later deletion of documents cannot be distinguished from the current index state; no index-level write or delete history was available.
The change-history integration is not configured in this Run, so no record of who or what recreated the pods at 2026-11-23T14:36-14:38Z could be checked.
No documents exist in app-189-metrics-timeseries before 2026-11-21T18:47:00Z (42 docs equals the full docs.count), so any earlier collection gaps, and the true start of collection, are unknown.
@timestamp is the writer's timestamp, so the exact moment collection stopped lies somewhere between 2026-11-23T07:47:00Z and the first missing 08:47:00Z sample and is not pinned down more precisely.

Check node or durable system logs for 2026-11-23T07:47-14:38Z to establish when the previous cluster and collector were shut down.
Review change history, unavailable in this Run, for any teardown or recreation of the cluster at 2026-11-23T14:36-14:38Z, which lines up with resumption of data at 14:47:00Z.
Validate the generator that produces request_id values to explain the off-pattern REQ-37-8A4F2 record written immediately before the gap.

notes: This tool has no time range: it shows the cluster's indices and mappings at the moment of the query, which can be after the authorized window.
view.cannot_prove: This is the state at the moment of the query only: it cannot prove which indices, fields or document counts existed during the incident window, nor that any document lies in that window. A field that is mapped is not proof that documents carry it.

Objects are the cluster's state when the query ran, not during the incident window: they cannot prove what was true earlier, and an object missing now may have existed then. Events cover only their own timestamps inside the window; an event that is not returned is unknown, not proof nothing happened (events expire and timestamps are often null). A jq result is what the expression selected, not a full picture of the kind. When the API server returns zero objects of a kind other than events (every page read), the result is ok with total_items_processed 0: it proves only that there were no objects matching this kind, namespace and selectors at query time, not that none existed during the incident. Zero events, or a list your filter reduced to nothing, stays no_data. metadata.managedFieldsSummary gives each manager's last write time only: it is not a full change history (earlier writes by the same manager are gone) and it does not say which fields that write changed.
